Chernobyl - In times of War

By: Floris Kotze | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We follow up on previous Chornobyl inserts. This time we visit the most famous nuclear disaster site during a war and ask, why is Chornobyl so important to the Russians?

Unique Selling Point:
Understanding the risks associated
with the site’s current condition and
the consequences of its occupation by
Russian forces in February 2022.

Summary:
Nuclear Safety at Risk:
Russian Acts on Chornobyl
It's a site most people avoid, yet the Russians are actively trying to occupy it? Why is this and what would they gain. We join a press group and visit Chornobyl for a full day - hearing exactly why it is so important to keep it out of the Soviet's hands.

Further information:
Captured by the Russians on 7 March 2022, it was reported that around 300 people (100 workers and 200 security guards for the plant) were trapped and had been unable to leave the power plant since its capture. On 31 March, it was reported that most of the Russian troops occupying the area had withdrawn. We go inside the exclusion zone and speak to experts as to why Chornobyl should be kept out of the hands of Putin.

Script:


Opening:
Upsounds / News
UPSOUNDS:
“This morning the Chernobyl nuclear site in Ukraine is now under the control of Russian troops.
And in March this year during Russian occupation, this is where some of the Ukrainians were held.
And all of this is coming under the shadow, of course, of what happened in Chernobyl decades ago 30 Kilometre Chernobyl Exclusion Zone”


VO:
April 1986. A CATASTROPHIC nuclear explosion in the THEN Soviet Union, shocks the world! What followed was UNLIKE anything we had ever seen: the evacuation of over 100,000 people from the Chernobyl area. Radioactive fallout spread far and wide, contaminating MILLIONS of acres and affecting countries as far as Sweden.

Thousands died from radiation-related illnesses, with countless more suffering SEVERE health issues.
Today, it remains one of the most radioactive places on Earth, with some estimating it won't be safe for another 20,000 years.
It led to the creation of what is known as an “Exclusion Zone” - An area surrounding the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant that extends from this part of Ukraine into Belarus. It is strictly controlled to limit human exposure to radiation.


Opening Link:
So we've been given permission to go to an area where not a lot of journalists go.
And this place grabbed the world's headlines before Russia even invaded.
And then, again, when the Russian troops occupied it.


VO 1: In February 2022, Russian armed forces seized Chernobyl.
They withdrew at the end of March, leaving behind a trail of devastation.
As the war rages, Chernobyl remains off-limits to all except essential plant employees. But we were given a rare opportunity along with a small group of other journalists to travel to the Exclusion Zone and speak to those impacted by Russia’s occupation.

Upsound
It's a security perimeter of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant and we are strictly forbidden to take any pictures and video of the perimeter because it's a very safe object…




VO 2:
First stop is the home of 82-year-old Halyna Viktorivna.
Her family returned here 16 years after the Chernobyl disaster.
I want to hear all about life under occupation, BUT she says that can wait.
First she insists I try her homemade kompott, a traditional Slavic fruit drink.

Govan:
What was it like on the first day?
Halyna:
Well, on the first day, they started walking around the yards. The patrol came to us, broke the gate, told the dogs not to bark at them and started looking around. But they did not enter the house, did not touch anything. They asked for cigarettes and asked for food. They said that if you leave the yard, put on white bandages, then our snipers will know that they should not shoot at you.

VO 3:
Across from Halyna's house is an unremarkable building, easy to overlook. Inside, though, vital tasks crucial to the exclusion zone are performed. THEIR accounts reveal a harrowing side to the Russian occupation.

GOVAN Link:
The first thing they've given me is this…
It's a Geiger counter.
And it monitors how much radioactivity I'll be exposed to during my stay here.
They say it shouldn't be more than a one and a half hour flight.

VO 4:
Most people think of the exclusion zone as a desolate, forgotten place, but Chernobyl is a critical nuclear storage facility for Ukraine.
Employing more than 4000 people, it’s where waste from other facilities is safely stored.
Dangerous tasks are handled in the nondescript building, like testing and monitoring radioactivity levels throughout the exclusion zone.
We're told this building was of particular interest to the Russians.

Olexandr Barsukov
The first impression was that it was terrible.
First of all, there were three floors.
Everything was destroyed, scattered, broken.

VO 5:
For weeks during the occupation, hundreds of Ukrainian workers were held hostage. Many refused to flee, working tirelessly out of fear of another nuclear disaster. When the Russians finally retreated the full extent of the damage was revealed.
Deputy Director of the Chernobyl Ecocenter, Olexandr Barsukov, was among those cleaning up.

Olexandr Barsukov
In every room, there were a bunch of excrement, a bunch of junk.
They were living there and making a mess of themselves.
I don't know what kind of people they were.
It was impossible to get in.
Govan:
So they looted this facility?

Olexandr Barsukov
All the computers were ripped open.
All the hard drives were pulled out.
Everything was scattered.
As far as I understand, there were their experts here who understood a little bit about it.
And there was a rumour that we were making a dirty bomb here. They thought that we were
making radiation weapons here.

VO 6:
The Russians caused more damage than just to computers and labs.

Olexandr Barsukov
My understanding is that they dug trenches in the Red Forest, Red Forest is an area that were isolated because of radioactive waste. there they must have received very large doses of radiation, because they dug up almost the waste itself.

VO6b
The "Red Forest," one of the most contaminated places on Earth.
After the 1986 disaster, the forest was covered with soil to contain radiation. But the Russian troops disturbed this delicate balance, increasing radiation levels tenfold.
According to reports, several soldiers suffered from radiation sickness.

Air Siren Link
We're looking at some of the damage done by the Russian troops here in Chernobyl and an air siren is just going off the usually sound them when a Russian plane that has bombs that could hit these targets has taken off it really puts us on edge but the ukrainians seeing used to it.

Chernobyl
Lubov Syvoraksha
I don't know what to say, Honestly, I hate them all. I hate them, that's easy to say. Well a normal person would not do such a thing.


VO 7:
Lyubov Sevoraksha harbours a deep hatred of Russia.
Her son Denys was taken as a prisoner of war, along with 168 other National Guard servicemen - they were defending the Chernobyl plant at the time. It’s where Lyubov and her husband still work.

Lubov Syvoraksha
It's difficult now, because you understand that the guys are in terrible conditions. We know it from those who returned. There is constant torture, hunger, cold. They are tormented. They have to stand for days, and at night they can be lifted up. They stand, and they sleep with the light on, if they are allowed to sleep at all. //Yes, it can be very difficult, but we hold on and hope that soon we will hug our relatives.

VO 8:
As of this broadcast, nearly half of the prisoners have been released… but Denis remains captive.
The consequences of the occupation are still being felt two years after Russian forces withdrew from the exclusion zone.
The area is dangerously littered with unexploded weapons and land mines planted by departing soldiers.
Making it safe is a huge undertaking…

Govan Link:
So we’ve come to the end of the day in Chernobyl and it is time to find out how much Radiation I have been exposed to…
My good friend Anton here has the Geiger counter… and so Anton this will show… this is going to tell me…
This can tell you that you have been exposed to about 130 Roentgens all day.
So over 9 hours I was exposed to 100 micro Roentgens - its comparable to 1 hour flight…
Or 1 hour in a microwave?
NO NO YOU”RE WRONG!

Closing VO 9:
We leave behind Chernobyl’s infamous Number 4 reactor - watched over by a statue of the Greek god, Prometheus. Days after our visit, Ukraine hosted a multi-country peace initiative while Russia laid down ceasefire conditions Kyiv could never accept. This plant, the site of one of the world’s biggest man-made disasters, might yet see the return of Russian troops.

We're at the world's most famous nuclear power station and it's back under the control of the Ukrainian military.
Carte Blanche is one of the first television crews allowed into Chernobyl after it was captured by Russian forces.

In 2022, Russia captured the Chernobyl nuclear power station.

The Russians may have left Chernobyl, but the damage that they've done lingers on.

This time we visit the most famous nuclear disaster site during a war and ask, why is Chornobyl so important to the Russians? Unique Selling Point: Understanding the risks associated with the site’s current condition and the consequences of its occupation by Russian forces in February 2022. Summary: Nuclear Safety at Risk: Russian Acts on Chornobyl It's a site most people avoid, yet the Russians are actively trying to occupy it? Why is this and what would they gain. We join a press group and visit Chornobyl for a full day - hearing exactly why it is so important to keep it out of the Soviet's hands. Further information: Captured by the Russians on 7 March 2022, it was reported that around 300 people (100 workers and 200 security guards for the plant) were trapped and had been unable to leave the power plant since its capture. On 31 March, it was reported that most of the Russian troops occupying the area had withdrawn. We go inside the exclusion zone and speak to experts as to why Chornobyl should be kept out of the hands of Putin. 30 June 2024 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: Opening: Upsounds / News UPSOUNDS: “This morning the Chernobyl nuclear site in Ukraine is now under the control of Russian troops. And in March this year during Russian occupation, this is where some of the Ukrainians were held. And all of this is coming under the shadow, of course, of what happened in Chernobyl decades ago 30 Kilometre Chernobyl Exclusion Zone” VO: April 1986. A CATASTROPHIC nuclear explosion in the THEN Soviet Union, shocks the world! What followed was UNLIKE anything we had ever seen: the evacuation of over 100,000 people from the Chernobyl area. Radioactive fallout spread far and wide, contaminating MILLIONS of acres and affecting countries as far as Sweden. Thousands died from radiation-related illnesses, with countless more suffering SEVERE health issues. Today, it remains one of the most radioactive places on Earth, with some estimating it won't be safe for another 20,000 years. It led to the creation of what is known as an “Exclusion Zone” - An area surrounding the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant that extends from this part of Ukraine into Belarus. It is strictly controlled to limit human exposure to radiation. Opening Link: So we've been given permission to go to an area where not a lot of journalists go. And this place grabbed the world's headlines before Russia even invaded. And then, again, when the Russian troops occupied it. VO 1: In February 2022, Russian armed forces seized Chernobyl. They withdrew at the end of March, leaving behind a trail of devastation. As the war rages, Chernobyl remains off-limits to all except essential plant employees. But we were given a rare opportunity along with a small group of other journalists to travel to the Exclusion Zone and speak to those impacted by Russia’s occupation. Upsound It's a security perimeter of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant and we are strictly forbidden to take any pictures and video of the perimeter because it's a very safe object… VO 2: First stop is the home of 82-year-old Halyna Viktorivna. Her family returned here 16 years after the Chernobyl disaster. I want to hear all about life under occupation, BUT she says that can wait. First she insists I try her homemade kompott, a traditional Slavic fruit drink. Govan: What was it like on the first day? Halyna: Well, on the first day, they started walking around the yards. The patrol came to us, broke the gate, told the dogs not to bark at them and started looking around. But they did not enter the house, did not touch anything. They asked for cigarettes and asked for food. They said that if you leave the yard, put on white bandages, then our snipers will know that they should not shoot at you. VO 3: Across from Halyna's house is an unremarkable building, easy to overlook. Inside, though, vital tasks crucial to the exclusion zone are performed. THEIR accounts reveal a harrowing side to the Russian occupation. GOVAN Link: The first thing they've given me is this… It's a Geiger counter. And it monitors how much radioactivity I'll be exposed to during my stay here. They say it shouldn't be more than a one and a half hour flight. VO 4: Most people think of the exclusion zone as a desolate, forgotten place, but Chernobyl is a critical nuclear storage facility for Ukraine. Employing more than 4000 people, it’s where waste from other facilities is safely stored. Dangerous tasks are handled in the nondescript building, like testing and monitoring radioactivity levels throughout the exclusion zone. We're told this building was of particular interest to the Russians. Olexandr Barsukov The first impression was that it was terrible. First of all, there were three floors. Everything was destroyed, scattered, broken. VO 5: For weeks during the occupation, hundreds of Ukrainian workers were held hostage. Many refused to flee, working tirelessly out of fear of another nuclear disaster. When the Russians finally retreated the full extent of the damage was revealed. Deputy Director of the Chernobyl Ecocenter, Olexandr Barsukov, was among those cleaning up. Olexandr Barsukov In every room, there were a bunch of excrement, a bunch of junk. They were living there and making a mess of themselves. I don't know what kind of people they were. It was impossible to get in. Govan: So they looted this facility? Olexandr Barsukov All the computers were ripped open. All the hard drives were pulled out. Everything was scattered. As far as I understand, there were their experts here who understood a little bit about it. And there was a rumour that we were making a dirty bomb here. They thought that we were making radiation weapons here. VO 6: The Russians caused more damage than just to computers and labs. Olexandr Barsukov My understanding is that they dug trenches in the Red Forest, Red Forest is an area that were isolated because of radioactive waste. there they must have received very large doses of radiation, because they dug up almost the waste itself. VO6b The "Red Forest," one of the most contaminated places on Earth. After the 1986 disaster, the forest was covered with soil to contain radiation. But the Russian troops disturbed this delicate balance, increasing radiation levels tenfold. According to reports, several soldiers suffered from radiation sickness. Air Siren Link We're looking at some of the damage done by the Russian troops here in Chernobyl and an air siren is just going off the usually sound them when a Russian plane that has bombs that could hit these targets has taken off it really puts us on edge but the ukrainians seeing used to it. Chernobyl Lubov Syvoraksha I don't know what to say, Honestly, I hate them all. I hate them, that's easy to say. Well a normal person would not do such a thing. VO 7: Lyubov Sevoraksha harbours a deep hatred of Russia. Her son Denys was taken as a prisoner of war, along with 168 other National Guard servicemen - they were defending the Chernobyl plant at the time. It’s where Lyubov and her husband still work. Lubov Syvoraksha It's difficult now, because you understand that the guys are in terrible conditions. We know it from those who returned. There is constant torture, hunger, cold. They are tormented. They have to stand for days, and at night they can be lifted up. They stand, and they sleep with the light on, if they are allowed to sleep at all. //Yes, it can be very difficult, but we hold on and hope that soon we will hug our relatives. VO 8: As of this broadcast, nearly half of the prisoners have been released… but Denis remains captive. The consequences of the occupation are still being felt two years after Russian forces withdrew from the exclusion zone. The area is dangerously littered with unexploded weapons and land mines planted by departing soldiers. Making it safe is a huge undertaking… Govan Link: So we’ve come to the end of the day in Chernobyl and it is time to find out how much Radiation I have been exposed to… My good friend Anton here has the Geiger counter… and so Anton this will show… this is going to tell me… This can tell you that you have been exposed to about 130 Roentgens all day. So over 9 hours I was exposed to 100 micro Roentgens - its comparable to 1 hour flight… Or 1 hour in a microwave? NO NO YOU”RE WRONG! Closing VO 9: We leave behind Chernobyl’s infamous Number 4 reactor - watched over by a statue of the Greek god, Prometheus. Days after our visit, Ukraine hosted a multi-country peace initiative while Russia laid down ceasefire conditions Kyiv could never accept. This plant, the site of one of the world’s biggest man-made disasters, might yet see the return of Russian troops. Chernobyl PROMOS 21 sec Govan: We're at the world's most famous nuclear power station and it's back under the control of the Ukrainian military. Carte Blanche is one of the first television crews allowed into Chernobyl after it was captured by Russian forces. Olexandr Barsukov They thought we were making radioactive weapons And they thought we were making radioactive weapons here. 21 sec Govan: In 2022, Russia captured the Chernobyl nuclear power station. It was unthinkable. And when they eventually retreated, they took nearly 200 Ukrainian national servicemen with them. The Russians may have left Chernobyl, but the damage that they've done lingers on. 21 Secs Govan: In 2022, Russia captured the Chernobyl nuclear power station. By the time they retreated, radiation levels in the Exclusion Zone were 10 times higher. Upsound: In short, here are the tanks. Here are the tanks. 21 Secs Govan: Why did the Russians capture the Chernobyl nuclear power station? Were they looking for information or did they come to loot the station? Upsound: The area around the site is highly dangerous because of unexploded weapons and land mines planted by departing Russian forces. CHERNOBYL TEASER ONE VO: We travel to the world's most famous nuclear power station – Chernobyl - once occupied by Russian military… UPSOUND: Olexandr Barsukov - They thought we were making radioactive weapons And they thought we were making radioactive weapons here. VO: Now it’s back under the control of Ukraine. TEASER TWO VO: In 2022, Russia captured the Chernobyl nuclear power station. VO: Then Russia retreated from Chernobyl, but the damage had already been done. Now, we travel to the world’s most famous nuclear power station during the ongoing war between Ukraine and the Kremlin. TEASER THREE VO: In 2022, Russia captured the Chernobyl nuclear power station.By the time the military retreated, radiation levels in the Exclusion Zone were ten times higher. Upsound: VO: We travel to Ukraine for a closer look at the damage caused by the ongoing war. TEASER FOUR VO: Why did the Russians capture the Chernobyl nuclear power station? Were they looking for information or did they come to loot the station? Upsound: VO: We travel to the world’s most famous nuclear power station, to get some answers. TEASER FIVE VO: On the outside, life in Chernobyl almost looks normal. UPSOUND: VO: But two years since the Russian invasion, the damage caused by the Kremlin’s military forces, still linger.
